title: E-commerce Promotion Automation: From 8 Hours to 15 Minutes
excerpt: A production case study on centralizing multi-store promotion setup, reducing repeated campaign work from about eight hours to about 15 minutes.
author: Nguyễn Kim Thu
imageAlt: Four storefront workflows converging into one centralized promotion module, with setup time changing from about eight hours to about fifteen minutes

content.text: E-commerce promotion automation is useful only when it removes a real operational bottleneck. In one production environment I worked on, campaign setup across multiple storefronts took about eight hours because the same promotion work had to be repeated. A centralized promotion module reduced that setup to about 15 minutes and gave Marketing a way to publish through an administration tool instead of relying on repeated manual entry.

This case study explains that change without pretending the result came from a single clever script. The important part was deciding what should become one controlled workflow, what the surrounding systems already owned, and where validation and access control belonged. I will separate verified production facts from the broader engineering lessons I draw from them; proprietary promotion fields, endpoint names, database structures and campaign rules are intentionally omitted.
The production problem was repetition, not a missing button

At Vong Xanh, the e-commerce landscape included multiple storefronts such as xedap.vn, giant.vn, xedaptot.com and active.vn. Promotions were part of a wider operating system in which storefronts consumed business data while internal teams needed tools to manage products, prices, customers and campaigns. The cost appeared when a campaign had to be prepared across more than one storefront: the setup was repetitive enough that a promotion cycle could take about eight hours.

That eight-hour figure matters because it describes an operational constraint, not merely developer inconvenience. Repeated entry consumes the time of the people preparing a campaign, increases the number of places that must be checked, and makes every additional storefront more expensive to operate. The problem therefore was not simply that one screen was slow. The workflow itself duplicated ownership.
Why repeated entry becomes a systems problem

When the same business change must be entered several times, each destination becomes another opportunity for drift. Even without assuming a specific failure that was not documented, the structure is inherently harder to reason about: a team must remember which storefronts were updated, which version is current, and whether the campaign is ready everywhere. Adding another store multiplies that coordination cost.

This is the first general lesson from the case: before automating keystrokes, look for duplicated ownership. If several screens all behave as separate sources of truth for one business operation, automating each screen independently may only make the duplication faster. Centralization can be the more important design decision.
What changed: one promotion workflow owned the repeated work

The implemented change was a centralized promotion module used across multiple storefronts. Marketing could publish campaigns through the administration tool, and the campaign setup time dropped from about eight hours to about 15 minutes. Those are the verified production facts at the center of this article.

The administration layer around this work was not an unguarded form. The broader production tooling for products, prices, customers and promotions included validation and access control. That matters because workflow automation changes who can perform an operation and how quickly a mistake can propagate. Making an operation faster without preserving control would have been the wrong outcome.
Centralize before you optimize

A useful mental model is to treat the administration tool as the place where the business expresses one intent: prepare and publish a promotion. The storefronts should not force Marketing to repeat that intent simply because there are several destinations. Once the workflow is centralized, automation has a stable boundary: transform one approved business action into the updates required by the surrounding systems.
The promotion module lived inside a larger e-commerce system

The promotion work did not exist in isolation. In the same production environment, React and Next.js were used on the frontend, Node.js and NestJS were used for application services, and REST APIs connected storefront behavior with operational data. Node.js services synchronized stock, prices, promotions and orders from Odoo ERP.

That surrounding context explains why a promotion management system must respect system boundaries. Odoo already participated in operational data flows; storefronts already consumed data through APIs; internal users already needed administration interfaces. The promotion module therefore belonged to a system of responsibilities rather than to one isolated page. I am intentionally not claiming an undocumented endpoint topology or database design here.

content.text: Implementation boundaries matter more than invented technical detail

A case study becomes less useful when it fills missing information with impressive-sounding internals. I do not have a source that documents the exact promotion payload, the names of individual endpoints, the persistence model, the retry policy or every campaign rule from this production module. So those details are not presented as facts.

What can be discussed safely is the boundary implied by the verified system: a controlled administration workflow, validation and access control, API-backed services, Odoo integration in the wider e-commerce stack, and multiple customer-facing storefronts. That is already enough to reason about several engineering decisions without pretending to reconstruct proprietary code.
General design lessons I would preserve in a similar system

First, validate before fan-out. If one business action can affect several storefronts, rejecting incomplete or invalid input before distribution is cheaper than discovering problems after partial publication. This is a generalized engineering lesson; it is not a claim about the exact validation rules used by the original module.

Second, keep authorization near the operation that changes business state. A centralized tool can remove repetitive work, but it also concentrates capability. Access control is therefore part of the product design, not an afterthought. In this case, access control is supported by the production experience; the exact roles and permission matrix are not documented in the available source.

Third, make the integration boundary observable. When Odoo, application services and storefronts exchange operational data, teams need to know whether a failure belongs to the source data, an API response, stored application data or frontend behavior. That debugging habit was part of the same production work: incorrect stock or price displays were traced across Odoo, API responses, stored data and the frontend before the responsible layer was fixed.
Before and after: the operational difference

Before: campaign setup across multiple storefronts involved repeated entry and took about eight hours. The operation was expensive because the same business intent had to be carried through more than one place.

After: the promotion workflow was centralized in an administration module, Marketing could publish through that tool, and setup took about 15 minutes. The reduction was not achieved by asking people to type faster; it came from removing duplicated execution from the workflow.

Eight hours is 480 minutes. Comparing 480 minutes with 15 minutes gives a derived reduction of 465 minutes per setup, or about 96.9 percent. That percentage is simple arithmetic from the two verified time estimates, not a separately measured production KPI, so I would not present it as an independent business metric.
What I would not claim from this result

I would not turn the time saving into unsupported claims such as zero errors, perfect data accuracy, fully autonomous campaign management or a specific revenue increase. None of those outcomes is established by the source available for this case. The strongest result is already concrete: a workflow that had taken about eight hours was centralized and reduced to about 15 minutes while giving Marketing a direct administration path.

Keeping that boundary is important in technical writing. A portfolio case study should show enough system thinking to explain why the solution mattered, while making it obvious which numbers came from production and which conclusions are engineering interpretation.
Practical takeaways for e-commerce workflow automation

Start with the operational path, not the framework. Measure where people repeat the same business intent, where responsibility is duplicated and which steps exist only because systems are separated. A slow workflow may be a UI problem, but it may also be an ownership problem disguised as data entry.

Choose one place to own the business operation. In a multi-store environment, that often means an administration workflow that can apply the same approved intent across destinations. The exact implementation may be a service, job, queue or direct API call, but those details should follow the domain boundary rather than define it.

Preserve controls while removing effort. Validation, permissions and clear failure boundaries become more important as automation gains reach. The goal is not maximum automation. The goal is a workflow that is faster for the business and still understandable when something goes wrong.
The real optimization was deleting repeated ownership

The most useful part of this case is not the 15-minute number by itself. It is the shape of the change: multiple repeated campaign operations became one managed workflow. Once ownership moved into a centralized promotion module, the technology could serve the process instead of forcing the process to mirror the technology.

That is the principle I would carry into another promotion management system, inventory tool or internal platform: understand the repeated work first, decide where the operation should belong, then automate within that boundary. A shorter workflow is the visible result. A clearer system of ownership is what makes the improvement sustainable.
